dhq:abstract.p: Digital reconstruction is often understood primarily as a means of preserving and increasing access to cultural heritage. This article argues that digitization also transforms the conditions through which cultural sites become knowable. Using the Ajanta Caves as a case study, it examines digital reconstruction through three related concepts: translation, simulation, and epistemic reconfiguration. Translation describes the selective transfer of material and spatial information into computational form; simulation concerns the modelling of selected dimensions of spatial and sensory experience; and epistemic reconfiguration identifies the broader transformation produced when these representations become searchable, comparable, and computationally organized. Drawing on digital humanities, digital heritage, archival, and Library and Information Science scholarship, the article examines how digitization affects spatial context, visibility, narrative sequencing, and interpretive authority. It argues that digital reconstruction is neither a transparent copy nor merely a substitute for the physical site, but a distinct epistemic object. The article concludes with methodological considerations for more reflexive digital cultural-heritage practice.

div.head: 1. Introduction: Ajanta Caves as an Epistemic Problem
div.p: Digital reconstruction has become an increasingly important means of documenting, preserving, interpreting, and providing access to cultural heritage. High-resolution imaging, three-dimensional scanning, virtual walkthroughs, and immersive environments can make fragile or inaccessible sites available for forms of study and engagement; otherwise they are difficult, and sometimes impossible, in their physical settings to study. Yet the transformation of material heritage into digital form raises a question that extends beyond preservation and accessibility: what happens to knowledge when a culturally and spatially situated object becomes a computational one?

This question is particularly significant for heritage sites whose meanings are constituted not only by visual content but also through material presence, bodily movement, spatial sequencing, illumination, sensory orientation, and historically situated forms of engagement. Digital environments can preserve and intensify certain kinds of information while reorganizing the conditions through which that information is encountered. As argue in broader digital heritage research, digital environments do more than transmit information; they mediate heritage by reorganizing its ontological and epistemological conditions. Similarly, studies of digitally mediated heritage experiences demonstrate that knowledge production in digital environments is shaped by data structures, interface architectures, and forms of user interaction rather than by material encounter alone . Digitization, from this perspective, is not simply a technical act of reproduction; it is also an epistemic intervention.

The Ajanta Caves provide a particularly productive case through which to examine this problem. Located in present-day Maharashtra, India, the Ajanta Caves comprise a series of rock-cut Buddhist cave monasteries and prayer halls excavated between the second century BCE and the sixth century CE. Carved into a horseshoe-shaped cliff overlooking the Waghora River, the site integrates architecture, sculpture, and mural painting into a continuous sacred environment. The painted cycles, including narratives from the Jātaka tales and scenes from the life of the Gautam Buddha, unfold across interior surfaces. They are designed for monastic dwelling, ritual practice, and devotional viewing.

The Ajanta Caves have long been studied as masterpieces of ancient artistic and religious expression. Their monumental rock-cut architecture and intricate mural cycles have established the site as a locus of art history and Buddhist studies. Rather than approaching the site solely as an object to be preserved, this article understands Ajanta as an epistemic environment. They should be looked as an embodied field of meaning that emerges through spatial, sensory, and narrative entanglements.
Ajanta Caves do not simply display meaning; it produces it through contingent interaction of body, space, light, and story. This layered interaction is schematically represented in figure 1.

The experience of Ajanta Caves is inherently situated; the sequence of chambers and sculptural foci generates an interpretive flow. They create light and shadow shape perception; visual attention to Jataka tales unfolds across surfaces and registers. These features work together to create architecture of knowledge that can be read and felt in ways that lie beyond visual documentation alone.

Yet many of these epistemic conditions are now difficult to access fully. Some Caves are closed for safety or conservation reasons, limiting both physical access and the embodied experience they once afforded. In response, digital documentation initiatives have proliferated. Projects range from immersive virtual walkthroughs to VR reconstructions and extensive 3D scanning efforts that render Ajanta Caves’ architecture and decorations into data form. have recently documented such initiatives for Ajanta Caves specifically, including experimental VR heritage systems intended to provide mediated experiences of the site’s visual and spatial dynamics. These digital forms offer access to enormous detail and new kinds of interpretive leverage, pixel-level representations, interactive navigability, and quasi-immersive environments but they also instantiate knowledge in ways that depart from embodied onsite experience.

The significance of this shift lies not simply in the difference between physical and virtual experience. It lies in the transformation of the conditions under which Ajanta becomes knowable. What does it mean to digitize knowledge that was originally constituted through bodily movement, spatial sequencing, changes in illumination and affective engagement? When spatially embedded murals become searchable images, architectural sequences become navigable interfaces, and material surfaces become computational datasets, the object being studied is not merely transferred from one medium to another. Its structures of visibility, access, sequence, and interpretation are also reorganized.

Understanding digitization in this way reframes Ajanta Caves not simply as an endangered cultural site in need of preservation techniques but as a site of epistemic transformation. Digitization might be framed as translation mapping features from one medium into another or as simulation, attempting to recreate perceptual or spatial conditions in a new environment . But these are not neutral moves, they alter both what can be known and how it is known. As indicate in their analysis of developments in digital cultural heritage research, digital technologies increasingly reshape the structures through which cultural heritage is accessed, interpreted, and mediated. In the context of Ajanta, these processes redistribute interpretive agency across institutions, interfaces, computational systems, and users, while generating forms of visibility and accessibility that differ from those of the physical site.
Against this background, this article asks three core questions:

list.item: What does digitization do to knowledge?
And in what ways can digital reconstruction be understood as translation, simulation, or a more radical epistemic reconfiguration?

div.p: These questions foreground not the utility of digital heritage technologies, but their epistemic consequences for how Ajanta Caves are known, experienced, and communicated across contexts. The central argument is that digital reconstruction does not simply reproduce the Ajanta Caves; it reorganizes the epistemic conditions under which the site is known. The article develops this argument through a conceptual distinction among translation, simulation, and epistemic reconfiguration. While translation emphasizes the transfer of cultural material across media and simulation emphasizes the recreation of experiential conditions, epistemic reconfiguration draws attention to the more fundamental changes produced when material, spatial, and embodied knowledge becomes computationally structured.

Ajanta therefore functions in this article not as an isolated example but as a case through which a broader Digital Humanities problem can be examined: how digitization changes the architecture of knowledge itself.

div.head: 2. Theoretical Framework: Digital Epistemology and Mediation
div.p: If Ajanta Caves is to be treated as an epistemic problem rather than merely a heritage site, the analysis requires a clear conceptual vocabulary. This section outlines three interrelated frameworks: knowledge as embodied and situated, digital mediation as an epistemic act, and reconstruction as translation, simulation, or epistemic reconfiguration. Together, these frameworks establish the conceptual basis for examining what changes when an embodied and spatially situated cultural environment is transformed into a digitally structured object.

div.head: 2.1 Knowledge as Situated and Embodied
div.p: The premise that knowledge is situated rather than abstract has deep roots in phenomenology and critical epistemology. account of embodied perception argues that meaning emerges through bodily engagement with the world rather than through detached cognition. Space is not a neutral container but a lived field structured through movement, orientation, and sensory modulation. Later developments in spatial theory, particularly formulation of socially produced space, reinforce the claim that spatial arrangements encode social and symbolic relations. Knowledge, therefore, is inseparable from the spatial and bodily conditions through which it is experienced.

Sacred architecture intensifies this relationship. As work on sacred space suggests, ritual environments do not merely house belief; they organize cosmological knowledge spatially. Architectural sequencing, thresholds, gradients of light and acoustic resonance structure how meaning is disclosed. More recent architectural phenomenology has emphasized how scale, material texture, and illumination produce affective and cognitive orientations that exceed discursive explanation .

In the context of the Ajanta Caves, these theoretical insights are particularly relevant. The Caves’ carved interiors, modulated light sources, and narrative murals depicting episodes from the life of Gautama Buddha generate knowledge through embodied progression rather than detached viewing. The pilgrim’s movement from exterior brightness to interior dimness recalibrates perception; the scale of sculptural figures reorients bodily awareness; narrative panels unfold across architectural surfaces. Knowledge at Ajanta is therefore environmental as well as visual or textual, emerging through the interaction of space, movement, sensory perception, and narrative.

Contemporary scholarship in embodied cognition by and further reinforces this position by demonstrating how perception and conceptualization are co-constituted through sensorimotor processes. This provides the baseline epistemological premise for the present study: when digitization transforms the spatial and sensory conditions through which a site is encountered, it also has the potential to transform the conditions through which that site is known.

div.head: 2.2 Digital Mediation as Epistemic Act
div.p: Digital mediation is often described as representational: a technological means of capturing and displaying preexisting objects. Yet scholarship in digital humanities and media theory increasingly challenges this assumption. argues that digital representations are not neutral reproductions but interpretive constructs shaped by interface design, data modeling, and visualization conventions. Likewise, demonstrates that digital environments are structured by database logic, privileging modularity, navigability, and recombination.

From this perspective, digitization is not merely technical translation but epistemic intervention. The process of encoding requires decisions about how an object is segmented, categorized, structured, and described; such decisions inevitably formalize interpretive assumptions. The practices of the Text Encoding Initiative (TEI) offer a useful example. TEI encoding does not simply format text; it identifies structural and semantic elements such as names, places, quotations, hierarchies; thereby rendering texts machine-readable and analytically tractable. Encoding becomes an act of structured interpretation.

The same principle applies to digital heritage environments. 3D scans, photogrammetric models, and virtual walkthroughs transform architectural surfaces into manageable datasets. Scholars in digital heritage such as have shown that such transformations reorganize ontologies of cultural objects. They shift cultural objects from material entities toward computational models that can be processed through algorithmic operations. Interfaces further mediate interpretation by structuring user pathways, enabling zoom, layering annotations, or rearranging narrative sequences.

This shift also raises a related question that becomes important for digital heritage and archival practice: what is the status of the resulting digital object in relation to the material object from which it is derived? A digital representation may preserve information about an original while simultaneously acquiring new structures, functions, and interpretive possibilities within a computational environment. The next subsection develops this problem through the concept of the digital surrogate.

The crucial distinction, therefore, is between representation and reconfiguration. Representation suggests fidelity to an original; reconfiguration acknowledges structural transformation. Digital mediation reorganizes scale, temporality, and navigability. It produces new regimes of visibility and invisibility. What appears on screen is conditioned not only by the site itself but by interface logic, software affordances, and data architecture. Digitization is thus an epistemic act: it shapes the conditions under which knowledge is produced, accessed, and validated.

div.head: 2.3 Digital Surrogates and the Problem of Representation
div.p: The concept of the digital surrogate provides an important bridge between archival and Library and Information Science approaches to digitization and the broader epistemological concerns of digital humanities. In archival practice, a digital surrogate generally refers to a digital object created to stand in for, provide access to, or reduce dependence on a physical original. Such surrogates can substantially extend access and support forms of preservation, research, comparison, and computational analysis that would otherwise be difficult to undertake. Yet the term also implies a relationship of substitution between original and representation that requires critical examination. , for example, demonstrates that the usefulness of a digital surrogate depends not simply on its existence as a reproduction but on the quality of its representation and the purposes for which it is used. Digitization consequently produces an object whose evidential and analytical capacities are shaped by processes of capture, conversion, processing, and subsequent use.

This distinction becomes especially significant when the materiality of the original contributes to its meaning. argue that physical archival objects and their digital surrogates communicate different forms of information because material characteristics do not transfer straightforwardly into digital form. A surrogate may increase visibility, accessibility, searchability, and manipulability while simultaneously altering or excluding qualities associated with scale, texture, spatial relation, bodily encounter, and material presence. The relationship between original and surrogate should therefore not be understood solely in terms of fidelity or loss. Physical and digital objects can enable different, and sometimes complementary, forms of knowledge. In the case of Ajanta, this distinction is particularly consequential because architecture, illumination, spatial sequencing, murals, and embodied movement function together as conditions of interpretation. A digital reconstruction may preserve substantial visual and spatial information while reorganizing the sensory and contextual relations through which that information was originally encountered.

Archival and information-science scholarship further demonstrates that the digital surrogate is constituted not only through image capture or three-dimensional modeling but also through description. Metadata, classification, segmentation, file structures, and descriptive systems determine how digital materials can be identified, retrieved, connected, and interpreted. emphasize the importance of metadata in establishing contextual information and supporting judgments of authenticity in digital archival environments, while also recognizing that representation necessarily involves decisions about what characteristics are included, excluded, or foregrounded. This reinforces the argument developed by Ciula and Eide (2016) that computational modeling is interpretive rather than neutral. A digital heritage object is therefore mediated at several levels: through the technologies of capture, through the structures used to encode and describe it, and through the interfaces and computational operations through which it becomes accessible.

Recent digital humanities scholarship pushes this distinction further. questions whether terms such as digital copy or digital surrogate adequately describe the ontology of digitized objects, arguing instead that digitization produces a selective description of the analogue object translated into computationally readable symbolic form. This formulation is particularly relevant to the present study because it shifts attention from resemblance to transformation. Once murals, architectural surfaces, spatial measurements, and descriptive information are encoded as structured data, the resulting object does more than stand in for Ajanta. observes that it can be searched, compared, enlarged, recombined, annotated, computationally analyzed, and encountered independently of the spatial and temporal conditions of the physical site. In this respect, scholars such as as well as argue that the digital surrogate begins to acquire what may be described as analytical autonomy, a possibility also implicit in critical discussions of digital heritage objects and archaeological data.

The concept of the surrogate is therefore necessary but insufficient for the argument developed here. It clarifies the representational relationship between a material source and its digital counterpart, while also revealing the limits of understanding digitization simply as substitution. The progression can instead be understood as one from material object to digital surrogate, from surrogate to computational representation, and from computational representation to a structured environment in which new operations and relationships become possible. At this point, the question is no longer only whether the digital object faithfully represents Ajanta, but how its computational organization changes what can be seen, connected, retrieved, compared, and consequently known. It is this movement from representation toward transformation that provides the conceptual basis for distinguishing translation, simulation, and epistemic reconfiguration in the following subsection.

div.head: 2.4 Translation, Simulation and Epistemic Reconfiguration
div.p: To clarify the stakes of digital heritage practices, it is useful to distinguish among three conceptual models: translation, simulation, and epistemic reconfiguration.

Translation refers to the transfer of content across media. In this model, digital reconstruction aims to preserve informational equivalence: murals become high-resolution images; architectural dimensions become measurable 3D coordinates. Translation assumes that meaning can be carried from stone to pixel without substantial alteration. Yet media theorists have long argued that no translation is neutral; each medium imposes its own constraints and affordances.

Simulation goes further by attempting to recreate experiential conditions. Virtual reality environments seek to replicate spatial immersion, scale, and sometimes even acoustics. Simulation foregrounds perceptual fidelity rather than informational accuracy. However, as scholar of simulation notes, immersive environments are structured by computational parameters that inevitably differ from material conditions.

Epistemic reconfiguration recognizes that digital reconstruction may generate a qualitatively new object of knowledge. Rather than reproducing Ajanta Caves, digital systems reorganize its accessibility, sequence, and analytical potential. They allow simultaneous comparison of murals across caves, spectral enhancement of faded pigments, or remote access detached from pilgrimage. The site becomes searchable, allowing forms of zooming, comparison, annotation, and retrieval that are not available through ordinary physical encounter. Knowledge shifts from ritualized progression to database exploration.

The three concepts therefore describe different degrees and forms of continuity and transformation. Translation emphasizes the movement of information across media; simulation emphasizes the reconstruction of experiential conditions; epistemic reconfiguration emphasizes the production of new conditions of knowing. This tripartite distinction clarifies the analytical vocabulary for the present study. The subsequent analysis therefore asks how digital reconstruction moves beyond translation and simulation toward epistemic reconfiguration, particularly when embodied sacred space becomes encoded, navigable, and computationally structured.

div.head: 3. Ajanta Caves as Epistemic Architecture
div.p: The preceding discussion established that digitization does not simply produce a substitute for a material object but creates a computationally structured representation through which new forms of access, analysis, and interpretation become possible. To understand what digital reconstruction transforms, it is therefore necessary to examine what the Ajanta Caves already accomplish as a structured environment of knowledge. Ajanta Caves are not merely a repository of paintings and sculptures. They constitute an epistemic architecture in which space, light, narrative, and embodied movement operate as interdependent systems of meaning production. Recent scholarship by and in South Asian art history and spatial humanities increasingly emphasizes the importance of architectural sequencing and environmental context in interpreting Buddhist cave sites. These studies move beyond iconography toward what may be understood as spatial hermeneutics, that is, an approach to interpreting how meaning is produced through the organization, movement, and sensory experience of space.
If knowledge at Ajanta Caves is structurally encoded, then it must be analyzed at the level of architectural organization and sensory choreography.

div.head: 3.1 Spatial Sequencing and Narrative Movement
div.p: Ajanta Caves are not isolated chambers but part of a deliberate topographical progression carved into a horseshoe-shaped escarpment. The movement from cave to cave generates narrative anticipation and ritual orientation. extensive chronological research demonstrates that cave construction and patronage unfolded in phases, yet the site ultimately produces a coherent spatial logic structured around devotional circulation.

Pilgrimage studies suggest that ritual movement functions as interpretive structuring . At Ajanta Caves, the physical act of entering, pausing, circumambulating, and exiting produces layered meaning. The visitor does not encounter murals as discrete framed objects but as surfaces embedded within columns, thresholds, and shrine chambers. Narrative panels unfold laterally across walls, requiring bodily repositioning to follow visual sequences.

In this sense, Ajanta Caves aligns with what architectural theorists describe as processional knowledge, where meaning is disclosed gradually through spatial unfolding rather than instant visual capture. The Caves therefore encode instruction through progression: movement through architectural space becomes part of the process through which knowledge is encountered and interpreted.

div.head: 3.2 Light, Darkness, and Visual Revelation
div.p: Light at Ajanta Caves are neither uniform nor incidental. The transition from exterior brightness to interior dimness requires physiological adaptation. As vision adjusts, murals emerge from shadow gradually. This perceptual recalibration is not merely optical but epistemic. work on sensory architecture underscores how light shapes temporal experience and cognitive orientation. Illumination becomes interpretive modulation.

Recent heritage science studies on ancient cave environments emphasize how low-light conditions alter color perception and spatial depth. In Ajanta Caves, limited natural light entering through carved façades produces shifting intensities across surfaces. Sacred temporality is embedded in this gradual revelation. Meaning is not instantaneously visible; it is disclosed through duration.

Scholars of Buddhist ritual architecture such as and have argued that interior darkness often signifies contemplative withdrawal and cognitive interiority. At Ajanta Caves, darkness does not obscure meaning; it conditions it. Perception is slowed. Attention is directed. The cave thus becomes a chamber in which visual restriction contributes to epistemic concentration.

div.head: 3.3 Murals as Narrative Cosmology
div.p: The mural cycles at Ajanta Caves, particularly the Jataka narratives recounting previous lives of Gautama Buddha, function as moral pedagogy embedded within architectural surfaces. Rather than linear panels separated by frames, scenes are distributed across continuous walls, requiring viewers to identify narrative cues through gesture, posture, and iconographic repetition .

Recent art-historical analyses emphasize that these visual programs operate as cosmological maps rather than isolated stories. They encode ethical exemplarity, karmic causality, and royal patronage within spatially layered compositions. Narrative episodes overlap temporally within single pictorial fields, complicating Western assumptions of linear storytelling.

Collective memory theory further illuminates this function. As argues, cultural memory is stabilized through material forms that endure beyond individual lifespans. Ajanta Caves’ murals operate as mnemonic architecture, sustaining doctrinal and ethical knowledge across generations of monastic and lay audiences.

Taken together, these features demonstrate that Ajanta Caves is not passive surface awaiting interpretation but an integrated knowledge environment structured through space, body, light, and visual narrative. Spatial sequencing guides narrative comprehension; light regulates revelation; murals encode cosmology and moral pedagogy; and movement activates knowledge. Understanding Ajanta Caves in this way clarifies what is at stake in digital reconstruction. What may be transformed through digitization is therefore not only the appearance of individual surfaces but the relationships among the spatial, sensory, and narrative conditions through which those surfaces acquire meaning.

div.head: 4. What Digitization Does to Knowledge
div.p: If Ajanta Caves functions as an epistemic architecture structured through embodied progression, calibrated light, and narrative layering, digitization does not merely preserve these features. It transforms the ontological and epistemological status of the site. What was once encountered through movement becomes accessed through interface. What required temporal adjustment becomes instantly retrievable. Rather than treating these changes simply as gains or losses, this section examines three related transformations through which digitization reorganizes knowledge of Ajanta: the conversion of site into data, the reorganization of spatial and narrative context, and the emergence of algorithmic visibility.

div.head: 4.1 From Site to Data
div.p: Digital heritage technologies such as 3D laser scanning, photogrammetry, LiDAR capture, and ultra-high-resolution imaging convert material surfaces into measurable datasets. In such processes, architectural depth becomes point clouds; pigment becomes color values; curvature becomes coordinate systems. As scholars in digital heritage have observed, digitization entails a translation of physical presence into computational abstraction.

This shift is not simply technical. It reorganizes what counts as knowledge. It changes the operations through which the site can be examined. The cave wall is no longer primarily encountered as textured stone in dim space; it becomes a manipulable 3D model that can be rotated, isolated, annotated, and archived. In digital environments, surfaces are disassembled into layers of data that can be measured independently of bodily scale. analysis of database logic is instructive here. Digital objects are modular and can be recombined, structured by underlying data architectures that privilege extraction and re-composition. When the Ajanta Caves are scanned, they enter this logic. The cave ceases to function exclusively as a contiguous experiential environment and becomes divisible into components that can be individually queried.

Recent digital archaeology literature emphasizes this transformation as a move from site to model, in which the digital surrogate acquires analytical autonomy . The digital Ajanta Caves is not merely a proxy for the physical Caves; it becomes a new object structured by metadata, resolution parameters, and computational affordances.

The consequence is not that embodied experience disappears, but that some dimensions of the site become detachable from the conditions in which they were originally encountered. Spatial relationships can be measured, surfaces compared, and architectural elements examined independently of the visitor's physical position. Digitization therefore expands the analytical mobility of the site while simultaneously loosening the relationship between knowledge and location.

div.head: 4.2 De-contextualization and Re-contextualization
div.p: Digitization does not only abstract surfaces into data; it also detaches murals and architectural elements from their original spatial sequencing. In the physical Caves, narrative panels are encountered through constrained bodily movement. The order of viewing is structured by architectural layout and light gradients. In digital platforms, however, images can be reordered, grouped thematically, or accessed through search queries.

Scholars of digital curation as well as have noted that interfaces act as interpretive frames, shaping pathways of engagement through menu design, hyperlinking, and tagging systems. When murals are presented in digital galleries or interactive walkthroughs, they may be reorganized according to iconographic themes, stylistic periods, or conservation status rather than architectural adjacency.

This produces a double movement: de-contextualization from the original spatial matrix and re-contextualization within interface logic. The user, rather than the architecture, determines sequence. Navigation becomes elective rather than processional. The ritualized pacing that once governed interpretation is replaced by click-based mobility.

observes that digital heritage research increasingly emphasizes that such reordering redistributes narrative authority. Authority shifts from architectural structure to curatorial metadata and user agency. The digital viewer may zoom directly to a specific Jataka scene, bypassing architectural thresholds that once mediated approach.

The result is therefore a transformation in the conditions of narrative interpretation. Knowledge becomes more accessible and more readily comparable: murals from separate Caves can be juxtaposed, individual scenes can be isolated, and thematic relationships can be established without following the physical sequence of the site. At the same time, narrative coherence is no longer anchored exclusively to architectural progression. Digital platforms introduce alternative pathways through which the site can be read, making interface organization and user navigation part of the interpretive process.

div.head: 4.3 Algorithmic Visibility
div.p: Perhaps the most consequential epistemic shift lies in algorithmic visibility. Digital imaging technologies enable forms of seeing unavailable in situ. High-resolution gigapixel photography allows magnification beyond what the naked eye can perceive in low-light interiors. Spectral imaging can reveal under drawings, pigment composition, and faded inscriptions invisible under normal conditions .

These technologies produce what might be described as epistemic surplus. Details occluded by time, soot, or environmental degradation become legible through enhancement algorithms. Color correction recalibrates faded surfaces. Infrared and ultraviolet imaging exposes layers otherwise concealed.

Media theorist argues that digital mediation generates new regimes of visibility governed by algorithmic processes rather than natural perception. In such regimes, what is visible is contingent upon software settings, enhancement parameters, and computational filtering. The digital image is not a transparent window but a processed construct.

For Ajanta Caves, algorithmic visibility means that murals can be examined at scales and depths impossible within the cave environment. Scholars can isolate brushstrokes, reconstruct damaged segments virtually, and analyze pigment distribution quantitatively. These capacities expand interpretive horizons.

Yet they also recalibrate the epistemic hierarchy between embodied and technological vision. What counts as authoritative knowledge increasingly derives from enhanced datasets rather than from sensory immersion. The digital does not merely replicate what was seen; it reveals what could not previously be seen.
The cave consequently becomes both a cultural and an analytical object: a site whose surfaces can be examined through forms of computational vision unavailable to the unaided observer.

Taken together, these three transformations demonstrate that digitization changes not only how Ajanta is accessed but the operations through which it can be known. Datafication makes the site measurable and modular; re-contextualization makes its elements available to alternative narrative pathways; and algorithmic visibility reveals features that exceed ordinary perception. The resulting digital environment therefore extends the epistemic possibilities of Ajanta while also introducing new structures of selection, sequencing, and visibility.

div.head: 5. Mediation and the Reshaping of Meaning
div.p: The preceding sections have shown how digitization converts a spatially and materially situated site into data, reorganizes its contextual relationships, and expands what can be computationally seen. The present section focuses more specifically on the interpretive consequences of that mediation: how interfaces frame meaning, how digital environments simultaneously flatten and intensify experience, and how access is redistributed alongside epistemic authority.

div.head: 5.1 Interface as Interpretive Frame
div.p: Interfaces structure the pathways through which users encounter digital heritage. Menu hierarchies determine what categories appear primary. Metadata tagging defines what is searchable. Curated thematic collections foreground certain narratives while keeping others in background.

has argued that graphical and interface forms are not transparent containers but capta, constructed representations shaped by interpretive assumptions. Similarly, and others in platform studies have shown how digital infrastructures encode epistemic priorities through technical affordances.

In the case of the Ajanta Caves, a virtual interface may allow users to browse murals by iconographic theme, historical period, pigment analysis, or cave number. Each pathway foregrounds a different interpretive dimension of Ajanta. A thematic menu privileges narrative content; a chronological filter emphasizes development; a conservation interface foregrounds material fragility.

Metadata tagging further structures interpretation. When a mural is tagged under Jataka, royal patronage, or Bodhisattva iconography, it becomes legible within those classificatory regimes. As scholars of digital archives note, metadata systems formalize interpretive acts into machine-readable categories . Tagging is therefore not merely descriptive; it is an act of framing.

Curated pathways extend this framing by replacing some forms of architectural sequencing with interface sequencing. Users may encounter Ajanta through clickable categories, thematic routes, or database searches rather than through the physical progression of the caves. The interface consequently becomes part of the interpretive environment rather than a neutral means of accessing it.

div.head: 5.2 Flattening Vs. Intensification
div.p: Digital mediation simultaneously flattens and intensifies experience. On the one hand, the immersive scale, acoustic resonance, and atmospheric density of Ajanta Caves’s interiors cannot be fully reproduced on a screen. The bodily recalibration required when moving from exterior brightness into interior darkness is replaced by a mediated visual field.

, a scholar of virtual heritage has repeatedly noted that digital representations often compress spatial and sensory complexity into visually dominant formats. The loss here is not merely aesthetic but epistemic: features of embodied and atmospheric experience may become less available even as visual information becomes more accessible.

Yet digital mediation also intensifies certain forms of analysis. High-resolution imaging enables close inspection beyond the capacity of in situ vision. Comparative analysis across Caves becomes immediate. Side-by-side juxtaposition of mural fragments allows stylistic and iconographic patterns to emerge that would be difficult to perceive sequentially on site.

This dual movement is central to the epistemic consequences of digitization: some dimensions of situated experience are attenuated, while others become newly available for analytical scrutiny. The digital environment therefore does not simply diminish the original experience; it changes the balance between embodied encounter and analytical mobility. This tendency reflects broader transformations in digital humanities scholarship, where computational affordances privilege pattern recognition, aggregation, and scale manipulation .

div.head: 5.3 Authority, Access, and Epistemic Redistribution
div.p: Mediation also redistributes epistemic authority. Traditionally, access to Ajanta Caves require physical travel and, in some cases, institutional mediation. Scholarship was conducted on site, often constrained by lighting conditions and preservation regulations. Digital platforms reconfigure this landscape by making high-resolution representations globally accessible.

This expanded access is frequently framed as democratization. Digital heritage initiatives aim to widen public engagement and reduce geographic barriers . Students, researchers, and general audiences can explore Ajanta Caves remotely. Access, however, should not be equated automatically with epistemic neutrality or equal authority.

When sacred space becomes globally navigable digital artifact, its meaning is subject to new interpretive communities. Scholars, curators, software developers, and users collectively shape its presentation. Platform governance, funding structures, and institutional priorities influence which features are highlighted and which remain marginal. Critical heritage studies remind us that such transformations are embedded in knowledge politics . Digital mediation therefore distributes access while also redistributing interpretive power. The representation of Ajanta becomes entangled with metadata structures, interface design, institutional priorities, and the wider infrastructure through which digital cultural heritage circulates.

The Ajanta that circulates digitally is consequently not identical to the Ajanta encountered in situ. It is a mediated cultural object whose meaning is shaped by the structures through which it is classified, accessed, and presented. The central issue is therefore not simply whether digital reconstruction increases access, but how the conditions of access participate in determining what becomes authoritative, visible, and knowable.

div.head: 6. Digital Reconstruction: Translation, Simulation, or Epistemic Reconfiguration?
div.p: The preceding sections have established that digitization changes not only the form in which Ajanta is encountered but also the conditions through which it becomes accessible, interpretable, and authoritative. The conceptual triad of translation, simulation, and epistemic reconfiguration can now be used to distinguish three dimensions of this transformation. They should not be understood as mutually exclusive stages. Rather, they identify progressively broader consequences of digital reconstruction: the transfer of material information into computational form, the modeling of spatial experience, and the reorganization of the conditions under which knowledge is produced. The transformation from material decay to digital stabilization can be understood as a structured pipeline.

div.head: 6.1 Reconstruction as Translation
div.p: At its most conservative reading, digital reconstruction operates as translation. The murals of the Ajanta Caves are converted into high-resolution scans, photogrammetric models, stitched panoramas, and color-corrected composites. Stone and pigment are transposed into pixels and polygons. This transfer, however, is not transparent. Like linguistic translation, it inevitably filters and reorganizes meaning.

Recent systematic reviews of virtual restoration practices by emphasize that reconstruction decisions involve algorithmic interpolation, conjectural completion, and selective enhancement. Missing fragments are digitally restored based on stylistic probabilities. Damaged surfaces are smoothed. Colors are recalibrated. What appears as recovery is often interpretive stabilization.

The limits of medium transfer are structural. Material properties such as scale, surface depth, mineral texture, and environmental decay resist full digital equivalence. The embodied act of approaching a dimly lit cave wall cannot be reproduced by screen-based representation. Even immersive panoramas, while detailed, remain framed by interface logic. Translation thus reveals its boundary: it produces legibility, but at the cost of material contingency and spatial embeddedness.
Digital Ajanta, therefore, is not the cave migrated intact into code. It is a computational representation produced through acts of selection, conversion, correction, and organization

div.head: 6.2 Reconstruction as Simulation
div.p: A second model frames digital reconstruction as simulation. Here the goal is not merely to convert but to immerse. Virtual reality environments reconstruct architectural space, lighting conditions, and even acoustic ambience. Users can “enter” Cave 1, navigate murals, and observe details otherwise inaccessible to the naked eye. Recent Study by and on immersive heritage platforms show how VR shifts spectators into participants, generating affective proximity and spatial agency.

Yet simulation confronts a deeper limitation. Ajanta Caves were not only an architectural environment; it was a sacred monastic space embedded in ritual temporality. The cyclical rhythms of Buddhist practice, the slow accretion of devotional presence, and the historical layering of repainting and decay formed part of its meaning. No immersive platform can fully restore this lived temporality.

Simulation can model spatial relations, lighting, movement, and selected sensory conditions, but it cannot reproduce the historical duration and ritual continuity through which the site acquired meaning. Virtual immersion therefore produces a form of spatial presence without reproducing the full temporal and cultural conditions of that presence.
Thus, while VR intensifies experiential access, it simultaneously abstracts the site from its ritual ecology. What it restores in visibility, it alters in temporality.

div.head: 6.3 Reconstruction as Epistemic Reconfiguration
div.p: The strongest interpretation moves beyond translation and simulation. Digital Ajanta Caves are not simply a copy of the Ajanta Caves in another format. It is a new epistemic object.

Digital reconstruction restructures temporality. High-resolution layering allows users to toggle between phases of painting, restoration hypotheses, and current conditions. Time becomes modular and reversible rather than cumulative. The cave is no longer encountered as a palimpsest shaped by erosion and preservation politics; it is reorganized into selectable historical states.

It restructures visibility. Enhanced zoom, spectral imaging, and contrast adjustments reveal iconographic details invisible on site. The authority of the “seen” shifts from embodied perception to computational augmentation. What counts as evidence is mediated through software pipelines.

It restructures authority. Curatorial decisions embedded in metadata, interface design, and reconstruction modeling defines which version of Ajanta Caves circulates globally. recent heritage research underscores, digital reconstruction involves interpretive hierarchies that privilege certain aesthetic or scholarly judgments over others. The digital model becomes a stabilized reference point, potentially overshadowing the unstable material original.

It restructures accessibility. While physical access to the Caves in Maharashtra is geographically and environmentally constrained, digital platforms distribute Ajanta Caves globally. This democratization expands pedagogical and research engagement. At the same time, it detaches the murals from their local custodial context, re-situating them within transnational digital infrastructures.

Finally, it restructures narrative sequencing. On site, movement through the Caves follows architectural progression. In digital space, navigation becomes nonlinear. Users can jump from mural to mural, cave to cave, bypassing spatial order. Narrative becomes database-driven rather than architecturally choreographed.

Taken together, these transformations explain why digital reconstruction should not be understood simply as secondary representation. The digital Ajanta circulates as a computationally structured knowledge environment in which material information can be searched, compared, layered, recombined, and encountered through interfaces unavailable at the physical site. The epistemic shift therefore lies not in technological novelty alone but in the reorganization of what can be seen, how it can be connected, and under what conditions it can be interpreted.

The distinction among translation, simulation, and epistemic reconfiguration is consequently one of emphasis rather than exclusion. Translation identifies the selective transfer of material information; simulation identifies the modeling of spatial and sensory experience; epistemic reconfiguration captures the broader transformation that occurs when those representations become computationally organized objects. For digital humanities, this final dimension is especially significant because it shifts the question from whether reconstruction is faithful to whether its methods, assumptions, and interpretive consequences are made visible.

div.head: 7. Conclusion: From Rock-Cut Knowledge to Encoded Knowledge
div.p: This study argued that the digital reconstruction of the Ajanta Caves should be understood not simply as an effort to preserve or reproduce a cultural site, but as a transformation in the conditions through which that site can be known. The movement from rock-cut architecture to computational representation involves successive processes of translation, simulation, and epistemic reconfiguration. Each process extends access to aspects of Ajanta while also altering the material, spatial, temporal, and interpretive relations through which its knowledge was originally constituted.

The analysis has shown that Ajanta is not merely a collection of architectural surfaces and images. Its knowledge environment is produced through the interaction of spatial sequencing, bodily movement, illumination, darkness, murals, narrative relationships, and historical and ritual contexts. Digitization makes many of these features newly accessible, measurable, searchable, and comparable. At the same time, it separates elements of the site from some of the conditions that gave them meaning. Digital reconstruction therefore creates neither a simple copy nor an uncomplicated substitute. It produces a computationally structured object with its own possibilities for interpretation and analysis.

This distinction has broader implications for Digital Humanities research. Digital cultural-heritage projects should therefore move beyond the question of whether a reconstruction is sufficiently accurate or visually convincing. Accuracy remains important, but it is only one dimension of the epistemological problem. Researchers should also ask what has been selected for capture, what has been transformed during processing, what has been excluded, and what new forms of analysis become possible after digitization. Such questions make the methodological assumptions of reconstruction more visible and help distinguish documentation from interpretation.

For practitioners undertaking digital cultural-heritage reconstruction, five considerations follow from the framework developed here. First, the conditions of the original site should be documented alongside the digital representation. Spatial relations, material characteristics, environmental conditions, and relevant historical or ritual contexts should not be treated as secondary information. Second, projects should distinguish between processes of capture and processes of interpretation. Scanning, photogrammetry, image enhancement, colour correction, interpolation, and conjectural reconstruction do not carry the same epistemic status and should be identifiable as different stages of the workflow. Third, computational transformations should be made as transparent as possible. Where algorithms, reconstruction assumptions, or enhancement procedures influence what users see, those interventions should be documented rather than hidden behind the appearance of visual completeness.

Fourth, digitization methodologies should preserve relationships rather than focusing exclusively on individual objects or surfaces. For sites such as Ajanta, the relationship between architecture, murals, spatial movement, light, and historical context is itself part of the cultural record. Metadata, linked data, spatial annotation, and interface design can therefore be used not only to describe individual elements but also to retain their contextual connections. Finally, researchers should treat the digital surrogate or reconstruction as an epistemic object in its own right. Its value lies not only in how closely it resembles the physical site but also in the new forms of inquiry it enables through search, comparison, visualization, annotation, simulation, and computational analysis.

These principles do not suggest that digital reconstruction should be regarded with suspicion or that its limitations outweigh its benefits. Rather, they encourage a more reflexive approach to digital cultural heritage. The strength of a digital reconstruction lies partly in its capacity to reveal dimensions of a site that may be difficult to examine through conventional encounters, while its limitations remind researchers that increased visibility does not necessarily mean complete knowledge. Digital Humanities practitioners should therefore design reconstruction methodologies that make both affordances and transformations visible.

The case of Ajanta consequently supports a broader proposition: when cultural heritage is converted into computationally organized data, digitization becomes an epistemic practice as much as a technical one. Translation transfers material information into another representational system; simulation models selected dimensions of spatial and sensory experience; and epistemic reconfiguration emerges when these representations become searchable, comparable, recombinable, and embedded within new interpretive infrastructures. Recognizing this progression can help Digital Humanities researchers develop reconstruction methodologies that are technically rigorous while remaining attentive to context, mediation, and the production of knowledge.

Digital reconstruction, in this sense, does not replace the rock-cut site. It creates another way of knowing it. The methodological challenge for Digital Humanities is to ensure that this new knowledge environment remains sufficiently transparent about what it preserves, what it transforms, and what it newly makes possible.
